Rendering: Lancia Delta Integrale Keeps the Hot Hatch Body Style But Looks Toward the Future Now
14 photos
Photo: car.design.trends / Instagram
When 2026 started, we heard about Lancia and its struggles – 2025 wasn’t the year of rebirth for the ailing Italian brand, and instead the relaunch wasn’t going as planned. Yep, just having an over-priced supermini isn’t enough to conquer Europe once again.
Lancia introduced the latest generation of the Ypsilon supermini in early 2024, their first new model in almost a decade and a half. However, the relaunch of the storied brand in export markets didn’t help with the dwindling sales, and the new model also didn’t have a positive impact – Lancia sold less than 12k units in 2025, down 64%.
The company had big expenses, too, as it returned to France, Spain, Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and Germany, but it’s possible that no one was duped by the expensive fourth-generation Ypsilon, especially since there are other Stellantis options at lower costs, like the Peugeot 208 and Opel Corsa.
No worries, though, as Stellantis devised a new strategy back in May and turned Lancia alongside DS Automobiles into a specialty brand managed by Fiat, while Citroen again started overseeing the premium French marque. Additionally, the company brought to the 2026 Paris Motor Show its second revival model, bringing back to life the storied Gamma – albeit not as a sedan but as a premium compact crossover SUV.
The fastback model is related to the DS No. 7 and 8 vehicles from DS Automobiles, as they all share the new STLA Medium architecture, and packs the latest technologies in the cabin along with a hybrid powertrain and no less than three all-electric variants rocking up to 375 horsepower and a range of up to 740 km (460 miles) for the middle EV model.
The flagship version is the all-electric Lancia Gamma HF Integrale, also returning to life the beloved HF and Integrale monikers, which became famous on the compact Delta model back during Lancia’s glory days of both passenger cars and motorsport. Obviously, this makes people dream about the latter once again, including the members of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI.
For example, good folks over at " car.design.trends " have recently focused our attention on a hypothetical proposal for a brand-new Lancia Delta by Andrey Bass, a virtual artist known as ‘basstocom’ on social media. Actually, he’s more than just a pixel master, as he’s been an exterior chief designer with brands like GAC, Lynk & Co, the Renault Group, and Infiniti.
Now he’s envisioning the return of the Lancia Delta Integrale , made famous with the various motorsport-focused incarnations of the Delta HF Integrale moniker. The CGI expert keeps the same body style as the historic model – a hot hatchback. However, now he’s looking toward the future rather than the past.
As such, we’re dealing with a three-door hot hatchback with slim horizontal LED headlights instead of double round ones, and the LED daytime running lights trickle behind them on the front fender flares. It’s an edgy treatment for the front fascia, complete with an extensive aerodynamic package, and now we’re apparently dealing with an EV since there’s no radiator grille or exhaust outlets around the back.
As for the profile, it’s quite muscular and edgy, while the rear is dominated by slim LED taillights and a massive wing at the top, along with a monster rear diffuser and bumper assembly. So, what do you think – yay or nay? View this post on Instagram A post shared by Car Design Trends (@car.design.trends)

News
Intel Panther Lake 18A At Computex 2025 2
Intel reported third-quarter 2026 earnings with revenue of $16.5 billion, up 21% year-over-year. Non-GAAP gross margin reached 44.1%, and non-GAAP EPS came in at $0.52. Data center demand is surging while the client PC business is struggling (mightily) under memory market conditions. We do not always cover these, but Patrick asked me to do this one because it shows a trend we have seen recently at STH.
Intel Q3 2026 Results Show Contrasting Segments
First off, at an overall level, Intel’s headline numbers are relatively positive. Up almost 21% Y/Y is good, but last year was not great for Intel.
Intel Q3 2026 Earnings Financial Highlights
The Data Center and AI (DCAI) group delivered $7.3 billion in revenue, up 78% year-over-year. David Zinsner, Intel’s CFO, called it Intel’s strongest data center revenue growth in 15 years. Segment operating income reached $3.0 billion with a 41.5% margin. One of the interesting bits on why we were covering this announcement is that the demand in the market has shifted towards AMD’s 192-core Turin parts, which Intel does not have a direct competitor for (maybe Clearwater?), but partners tell us that Xeon 6 is selling because basically everything is selling.
Intel Q3 2026 Earnings Data Center And AI
Demand is strong across hyperscale, enterprise, and neo cloud customers, with “Purpose Built Silicon” revenue more than doubling year-over-year. Lip-Bu Tan, Intel’s CEO, said Intel’s immediate priority is unlocking additional supply to meet extraordinary demand for the Xeon family. On the call, he said that substrate availability is limiting output and it would take some time to ease.
The client side looks very different. Client Computing and Physical AI Group (CCPG) revenue fell 5% year over year to $8.1 billion. Overall inflation is well north of zero depending on the index you use, so revenue falling is not good. On the call Intel cited industry-wide memory shortages impacting the total addressable market. Higher DRAM and NAND prices are pushing system costs up and hurting demand. On the call, it sounded like Intel was looking for 18A supply to be used on the data center side pending substrate availability.
Intel Q3 2026 Earnings Client Computing And Physical AI
Intel expects the PC slowdown to continue at least through the first half of next year. Memory and NAND pricing pressure is expected to persist into 2027, which means client system costs are likely to stay elevated for a while longer. For those who see today’s memory prices and think they are shocking, the earnings call commentary did nothing to make me think Q1 would see a decline in memory pricing.
Intel Foundry posted $6.7 billion in revenue, up 58% Y/Y, though that figure includes intersegment transactions rather than external customer sales alone. The segment still recorded an operating loss of $1.9 billion with a negative 27.7% margin, but that is narrower than the $2.3 billion loss a year ago.
Intel Q3 2026 Earnings Intel Foundry
Improved yields and cycle times are reducing wafer costs. Intel released the Intel 14A 0.9 process design kit in October as committed, and expansion continues across sites including Ohio .
Final Words
We do not cover all earnings calls, but Patrick’s thought was that this was an important one since it also tells a story of STH. Folks wonder why we have been doing a lot of AI desktop and server/ networking coverage, and fewer mini PCs. Intel’s Panther Lake is a cool product, but it is not running larger local models. Right now, DRAM and NAND are being priced for the value they bring attached to AI nodes. Likewise, the NVIDIA-Intel investment and the many NVIDIA GPU-based systems with Intel Xeon CPUs are helping drive Xeon 6 sales and push pricing up. As a result, we are seeing the market demand for non-local AI PCs drop due to higher prices, while the AI-related markets are cooking. We know folks want more mini PC reviews, but this is a fundamental industry challenge. A smaller client-side market also means fewer small companies trying to innovate on form factors, while the data center market is the exact opposite. This came out very clearly in Intel’s earnings.

This AVC RIG Camper Van Keeps Things Open and Roomy While Hiding a Shower in Plain Sight
22 photos
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / AVC RIG
Today's featured build is based on a 2025 Ford Transit High Roof Extended. It was brought to life by AVC RIG, a Loveland, Colorado-based company that specializes in van conversion kits and full camper van conversions. We've covered some of its work here on autoevolution, such as this versatile setup . AVC stands for Adventure Van Conversions.
As usual, let's first take a look at the exterior. Although it doesn't have that many exterior mods like we see on other rigs, someone who's familiar with camper vans will be able to tell that it's a mobile home.
The van rides on black Transit alloy wheels wrapped in all-terrain tires. Moreover, on the sides, you'll notice an AM Auto window and two CR Laurence half-slider windows.
The last important upgrades are on the roof. There's an AVC rack that holds a solar panel and a flat-mounted Starlink antenna. Furthermore, the roof integrates a Maxxair vent fan and a 48V A/C unit.
Other notable mods are power and water connections, an SAP port for the Starlink system, and side steps.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / AVC RIG Inside is where things become more interesting. As you enter, you'll notice that the interior has an open layout, with no wall separating the driver's cabin from the living space. The open layout, the small number of overhead cabinets, and the overall arrangement of the interior areas make the space feel very roomy.
Regarding aesthetics, the customer opted for AVC grey felt wall kits, a fabric trim with a different grey tone, a white ceiling, 2tec2 flooring, and glossy Azure Blue cabinetry. The look is complemented by a bright white solid surface countertop and some black accents, like the cabinet and drawer handles.
The driver and passenger seats came from the factory mounted on swivel bases, so they can be turned around to face the back of the van. The passenger seat base hides an Espar heater that's tapped directly into the vehicle's fuel tank.
If you want to enjoy a meal or work on your laptop in the cabin, you can set up a small table by using a Lagun mount. What's more, between the seats, you'll find an AVC locker.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / AVC RIG Straight ahead as you step inside, you'll come across the kitchen. It features a multi-function oven, a deep stainless steel sink with a cover, a dual-burner induction stovetop, and an IndelB fridge with a freezer compartment.
A large overhead cabinet, a cabinet underneath the sink, and a cutlery drawer are available for storage.
What looks like a massive lower cabinet behind the driver's seat is, in fact, a bathroom. Lift its hinged top and you'll discover a cleverly built shower setup. There's also enough space to add a toilet inside it.
On the opposite side, by the sliding door, AVC RIG fitted a single-person bench that offers storage space. Behind it, there's a counter offering a bit of surface area and four decently sized drawers.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / AVC RIG It has a Tetravan sprayer with a mixer and a pan underneath that drains into a tank on the bottom part of the van. To complete the shower setup, you must attach a curtain to the ceiling.
The rear part of the living space is taken up by a sleeping arrangement. It's a twin-bed setup, with each bed being 26 inches (66 centimeters) wide and 80 inches (203 centimeters) long. Of course, the beds can double as benches.
You get window cubbies on each side of this space, which offer a bit of room for storing bits and bobs, and also provide USB charging points. Above, there's a 48V Velit 2000R A/C unit that can quickly cool off the entire interior. The customer also requested to have four speakers integrated into the ceiling – and AVC RIG delivered.
The beds are also where the rig's utility systems live. Power is inside the passenger-side bench – the rig's electrical heart is an EcoFlow system with a 5 kW capacity that can be expanded to 10 kW.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / AVC RIG As for plumbing, the van is equipped with a 30-gallon (113-liter) freshwater tank installed over the wheel well, a 6-gallon (22-liter) water heater, and an under-mounted greywater tank. A small door on the rear part of the driver-side bed offers access to an outdoor shower system.
Finally, there are two Van Essential storage pockets attached to the inner part of the back doors. Furthermore, all the windows in the van come with shades from the same brand.
All in all, this custom creation by AVC RIG keeps an open, roomy feel while also packing a bunch of creature comforts that make it possible to travel off-grid – that's a combo that's hard to achieve.
Besides offering conversions, the company also sells conversion parts for multiple van models, including the Ford Transit and the Mercedes-Benz Sprinter. So, if you liked a specific component or setup in this rig, you might be able to find it on the company's website.

This Snow-Bound Porsche Mission S Looks Official – But There’s a Catch
6 photos
Photo: Instagram | onb.artdesign
The unveiling of the Porsche Mission S was clouded by the new Tesla Roadster demonstration, which made everyone and their grandmother speak about it, regardless of whether they are petrolheads or not, and creating a tsunami of AI videos and memes.
Coming nine years after it was unveiled as a study, the new Tesla Roadster is still not ready. That’s despite the fact that it should have been on the roads since 2020, though in plain Tesla fashion, it has been delayed multiple times. Now, the company says that it will be a thing in 2028, which is the study will turn 11, but to be honest, do you really think that it won’t be delayed again? Yeah, it probably will, and it will be interesting to see whether the gas thrusters will be a thing once it finally reaches dealers.
Nevertheless, we haven’t gathered here to talk about this model, but the Porsche Mission S mentioned in the intro, which came out a couple of weeks ago, just one day after it leaked online. This is one important machine for the Zuffenhausen brand, which proved that in the never-ending crossover / SUV chase, it can still drop some exciting rides. It offers a glimpse into a future super sports car that will top the 911, and also previews the brand’s future design identity, and between us, it’s definitely an eye-catching product, isn’t it?
Porsche’s Mission S has a familiar-looking front fascia, and from certain angles, the average Joe could easily mistake it for a more aggressive variant of the Porsche 911. And that’s definitely not bad, especially in this day and age when some cars have gone down the quirky side of things when it comes to their design. The Mission S features a vented hood at the front, a set of familiar-looking headlights, a very large vent in the lower part of the bumper, an apron with blades on the sides, and muscular wheel arches.
Photo: Instagram | onb.artdesign Further back, we can see that the roof is home to a scoop, and that the profile is both clean and aggressive at the same time. The back end is quite dramatic, for what it’s worth, as it features stuff such as a radiator fan in the middle of the engine cover, which reminds us of the Porsche 917 . The car also has a quite uncommon diffuser, as well as a flowing rear wing. The four stacked exhaust pipes are part of the styling, alongside the thin taillights separated by the Porsche lettering.
Thus, even though the Mission S is all about Porsche’s future, it remains easily recognizable as something that came from the Zuffenhausen-based company. And since it is a very important product for the automaker, it has clearly fallen into the hands of the rendering crowd. So far, we have seen it presented on different wheels in a few digital illustration sets, and this time, it’s something quite different that we have here.
You see, the wheels of this imagined Porsche Mission S are the standard ones, and that’s a good thing, in my opinion, anyway, because they look very good. What is new, though, is the roof rack, which has some skis strapped to it, thus proving that exotics can indeed be used for winter sports. Its maker, @onb.artdesign on Instagram, says that this machine is “the ultimate legend for a winter getaway,” ending up in the white scenery directly “from the slopes.”
Photo: Instagram | onb.artdesign The roof rack with a pair of bars is definitely something that you do not see everyday, especially on an exotic model, though deep down, we think that the Porsche Mission S would have looked a lot better if it had had a roof box. But hey, we won’t complain about the unofficial redesign, as the pixel-manipulating process has created something quite different here, and overall, this remains a head-turner, and a quite uncommon one due to the extras added to its roof.
Now, the Porsche Mission S may look like an EV, albeit a very high-end one with an obvious emphasis on fast cornering, and dizzying top speeds. However, the radiator fan mentioned above and the tailpipes are a clear indicator that we are looking at an ICE model. The company described it as “a mid-engined sports car platform positioned above the 911 – not as a one-off hypercar, but as a permanent and versatile addition to our customer offering,” according to Porsche boss Michael Leiters.
You are probably wondering what exactly powers this ride, and guess what? So are we! That’s because Porsche hasn’t detailed the oily bits of its Mission S. Still, we do know that the automaker is currently working on a powerful new eight-cylinder engine for its upcoming flagship model, and that one is expected to be the production version of the Mission S. Therefore, that’s what should power it, and we cannot wait to learn more details about this powertrain. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Onur Bakır (@onb.artdesign)

Hot Wheels News: 9 Premium Models Arriving in 2027
27 photos
Photo: Lamley Group
A little while ago I had the chance to buy one of Mattel’s old Hot Wheels Customized C3500 models. It was part of an Editor’s Choice series, and it had PC5 wheels on. I hesitated, and went back to the listing after two days only to find out it wasn’t available anymore.
It’s not the first time I’ve made a mistake like this. But I guess it happened for a good reason: I didn’t really like the livery. I also know this guy will keep on “unearthing” classic collectibles like it, as he’s been at it for a few years now. I still have a 10-pack from him that I haven’t opened yet, alongside 30 to 40 other premium-level cars waiting in my living room.
After 10+ years in the hobby, I am now more interested in older Hot Wheels than I am in the newer ones. However, Ronald Wong’s work has been quite effective in balancing the scales as he has worked on at least a dozen amazing castings over the past two years. And he’s got a few more aces up his sleeve, as you’ll see in the video at the end of this story.
I will only briefly walk you through the items inside that I’ve already discussed in previous stories, as I plan on focusing on the eight new cars most of you have likely never seen before. The first four sets of Car Culture are the starting point, and it seems like the first three ones are missing the fifth vehicle. For Mountain Drifters it’s the Itasha-themed Nissan Silvia S13.
Over in Exotic Envy it’s the Dodge Viper RT/10. Lastly, Canyon Warriors is missing the 2012 Mercedes-Benz C 63 AMG Coupe. Modern Classics is the big surprise here, and Ron pointed out that “Pop-up Headlights” is the theme here. I’d say that’s a bit of an overstatement considering all the headlights are down.
Modern Classics are back Photo: Lamley Group I’m sure some kids might even find it difficult to comprehend the concept of “pop-ups” considering manufacturers have long abandoned this solution. Anyway, I’m being nitpicky here, especially since I’ve had access to Tomica collectibles where you can use a switch to play with the headlights. We’re getting two new castings in this mix, and the 1990 Honda NSX is one of them. It’s still in an early phase of development, and it’s not that easy to tell how much different it is to Ryu Asada’s design.
That 2003 Type-R has been around since 2020, but it has somehow only had two distinct variations in all these years. Here’s to hoping Ron Wong’s First Edition release won’t be white or black (I’m betting on red). You’d think I’d be happy about the new RX-7 casting, given I’m a long time rotorhead. Jun Imai’s ‘95 model is a decade old at this point, and it’s slightly too tame for this tiny “universe”.
I was hoping for some RE-Amemiya, Fujita Engineering or Panspeed goodness, especially since the factory-spec Spirit R had already joined the Matchbox line-up a while ago. This just seems like an adaptation of that casting, but in a less exciting way than what happened with the McLaren F1 GT and F1 GTR duo which Mr. Wong was also in charge of. My only hope is that Titanium Gray Metallic won’t be the debut color, as it’s simply too predictable and not exciting enough for an RX-7.
The other obvious options are Innocent Blue Mica, Pure White, Brilliant Black and Vintage Red. I’m only buying one if it comes in Competition Yellow Mica, which is not likely to happen. I want to say that the Corvette is a new variation for Lindsey Lee’s ‘84 model, but I’m not 100% sure at this point. The MR2 is a replica of Ron’s real-world car, and I remember seeing a preview of it a few months ago.
Jerry is coming to Pop Culture Photo: Lamley Group At that point I had no clue what series it was intended for, which is no longer a mystery. Andres Andrieu also gets a replica of his real world Porsche in this set. It’s the second premium variation of this casting in a row, as it’s also part of this year’s Team Transport series where it’s sporting a Shell livery. Ronald didn’t want to disclose what the Chase collectible for the set will be, and we could speculate that either the NSX or the RX-7 will take on that role.
I have a better chance at buying Red Line Club models than Chase cars, so I won’t even bother looking for it. I haven’t seen any Pop Culture news in some time now, and I would’ve never expected Jerry’s car to be a part of this line.
I just recently bought Rick’s ship, and would love a closer look at some of the older Rick & Morty-themed collectibles in Mattel’s portfolio. I’m still a fan of the show, despite its decline over the years and ditching one of its two creators.
I can’t say this casting is iconic in any way to me, though, as I can’t even remember seeing it that often on screen. I’m more enthusiastic about the new C5 Corvette, and it’s fun to know that Hot Wheels designer Eric Han has one at home. It’s headed for the Premium Fast and Furious series, and I admit I had to Google it to find out which movie it was in. Wasn’t the one in 2 Fast 2 Furious a convertible?
Racing Culture is off to a great start Photo: Lamley Group Anyway, this thing won’t be nearly as desirable as the Porsche 911 RSR Turbo that’s headed for Racing Culture. It’s probably safe to assume the Martini look is first in line for it, and that the chances of finding one in the wild are minimal. The Pontiac Stock Car is another unexpected surprise, although I recall seeing a blurry image of it at one point.
There’s a good chance the First Edition will pay tribute to a similar, older Hot Wheels design, one that you might have also seen racing at Pikes Peak at some point.
I guess everyone has seen the next RLC Ferrari by now. Despite it not having any opening features, the execution on those seats and steering wheel is fairly impressive!

Stolen, Recovered the Same Day: 1969 Road Runner Packs the Holy Grail: Low Miles, 426 Hemi, 4-Speed
11 photos
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150
Deep in the timberland of Vernonia, Oregon, inside a historic brick building that originally opened as a Chevrolet dealership in 1938, longtime collector Gary Myers guards a deceptively understated two-door pillared coupe. It was, when new, in fact, the cheapest big-block intermediate from the cheapest division of the smallest of the Detroit Big Three. If it weren’t for those obscenely big, black valve covers, it wouldn’t be such a big deal. However, because of that detail, it is a big deal. The biggest of its day. A 1969 Hemi Road Runner.
When Mopars5150 host Troy Bergeron visited Gary's private workshop, they knew they were in for a treat of galactic proportions. And it’s not like he hasn’t had his fair share of muscle car greatness – that’s what he does for a living, after all. And yet, every time he sees one of those time capsules, he turns into a five-year-old left alone in the Hot Wheels factory, no holds barred. For good reason – any one of us would do the exact same thing.
A B5 Blue Fire Metallic 1969 Plymouth Hemi Road Runner that looks remarkably fresh through and through is Gary’s second rabbit out of the hat, after the impeccable, unmolested, untouched 1970 Plymouth Road Runner-Dodge Coronet mongrel, the Superbird.
Plymouth launched the Road Runner moniker in 1968 after paying $50,000 to Warner Bros. for the cartoon bird's likeness and spending $10,000 with Sparton to engineer its signature "beep-beep" horn. Designed as a stripped-down, affordable performance machine that could run a 14-second quarter-mile for less than $3,000, the nameplate enjoyed a 13-year production run from 1968 through 1980 across three distinct B-body generations and a final F-body Volaré platform.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 The 1969 model year marked the absolute zenith of the model's popularity, with Plymouth dealers delivering 84,420 Road Runners across three body styles, and three engine options: 33,743 were two-door pillared coupes, 48,549 two-door hardtops, and 2,128 convertibles. It was the first of the two years when a Road Runner would have a topless option.
Approximately 97 percent of those buyers kept the standard 383-cubic-inch (6.3-liter) V8, while 1,412 opted for the mid-year A12 440 Six-Barrel package, leaving the mighty J-code 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi V8 as the ultimate low-production rarity.
Rated conservatively at 425 hp (431 PS) at 5,000 rpm and 490 lb-ft (664 Nm) of torque at 4,000 rpm behind dual Carter AFB 4-barrel carburetors and 10.25:1 compression, the 426 Hemi found its way into only 788 Road Runners in 1969. It still was the best-selling Hemi Mopar model, but it was actually down from 1968 (when the Road Runner had premiered) during which time the 426-cuber weas ordered by 1,019 customers, making the 1968 Road Runner the only car and the only year where over 1,000 copies of the fabled motor were sold under a single moniker).
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 That 1969 total comprises 422 hardtops, 10 convertibles, and 356 pillared coupes; of those 356 lightweight post coupes, just 194 left the factory with the 4-speed manual transmission.
Bolted to the inner fender beside an original Chrysler Cleaner Air System decal, the factory fender tag confirms this coupe rolled out of Detroit's Lynch Road plant, with a scheduled production date of April 11, 1969.
The tag stamping isn’t lying – the Road Runner was a no-frills, all-thrills machine built to do one thing, but be the best at it, bar none. The small metal plate is mostly flat – only a few codes on the bottom telling that whoever ordered this car didn’t really care about much else except that big ogre upfront. A 426 Hemi V8 paired with a Coyote Duster Air Grabber fresh-air hood and a 26-inch heavy-duty radiator, and an 18-spline A833 New Process 4-speed gearbox.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 Most notably, the A34 Super Track Pak - with its 9.75-inch Dana 60 with a Sure-Grip rear axle hiding 4.10:1 gears - indicates that the car was aimed squarely at quick-quarter supremacy (sanctioned of not, on and off the road/track). 10-inch rear drums and rare power front disc brakes made the most of the stopping power available in the period.
The early life of Gary's 1-of-194 Hemi 4-speed coupe reads like a Hollywood crime thriller. Ordered new in Virginia by a French-named gentleman called Sierra Petty who suffered from a bad foot, the car was supposed to arrive with an automatic transmission. When the dealership unloaded a 4-speed manual car instead and told him it was too late in the 1969 model year to reorder, he reluctantly took the clutch-equipped coupe home.
Shortly thereafter, thieves stole the Hemi Road Runner from an A&P grocery store parking lot and spirited it away to a local chop shop. Working feverishly, the criminals cut the radiator core support out of the nose and yanked the 426 Hemi V8 from the engine bay. Moments later, police raided the facility—finding it packed with stolen big-block Corvettes—and recovered the Plymouth with its matching-numbers Hemi sitting beside it.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 Reassembled and returned to the road, the blue survivor migrated south to Sarasota, Florida, where a subsequent owner traded a Dodge Viper to acquire it, before the coupe landed in Dallas, Texas with just 19,000 miles (30,578 kilometers) on its odometer. Because its April 11, 1969 build date fell after the January 1969 federal safety mandate, it features factory head restraints, and it retains its original factory B5 Blue paint inside the trunk, door jambs, and engine bay.
Gary's acquisition of the car in the summer of 1999 hinged on a lucky typographical error. While browsing eBay during his lunch break for 1:18-scale diecast models, he spotted the Texas Hemi coupe and spent weeks calling the seller to verify the H9 glovebox inspector stamp and Dana 60 rear axle markings. When the auction closed, Gary tried to bid $10,000, accidentally typed a comma into the bid box, and watched his bid fail.
Devastated and holding pre-planned airline tickets in his hand, Gary received a phone call from the seller 30 minutes later. The winning bidder had turned out to be a serial internet deadbeat who had just defaulted on vintage Duncan yo-yos and sports tickets. Gary flew to Texas on July 3, 1999, closed the deal, flew home in time for July 4 fireworks, and paid $2,000 to have it trailer-delivered on July 6.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 With 20,700 miles (33,313 kilometers) now showing, Gary describes driving the manual-steering, bias-ply-shod coupe with 4.10 Dana gears as "herding a pig with a stick." After adjusting the solid-lifter valves and timing, he once blasted down Woodburn Dragstrip in 12.5 seconds at 112 mph (180 kph) through closed exhaust, and later nearly wrecked the survivor when it broke traction sideways at 80 mph in third gear during an impromptu race.
More like herding a boar with a straw of hay. Except the pig is on steroids, caffeine, had an argument with the wife, and his favorite team lost the Superbowl. That’ probably why it sits in a showroom – a former Chevrolet showroom, at that – instead of in a garage or out on the street.

Remembering the B Turtle Bike Microcaravan: The Tiniest RV You Could Tow by e-Bike
33 photos
Photo: YouTube/Atik Family
The road to hell is paved with good intentions, broken dreams, failed startups, and amazing products that fail to catch on. Among them is the B Turtle, a bike microcaravan once in the running for the title of the world's smallest RV.
Technically, it wasn't an RV but a towable. B Turtle was an inflatable microcaravan designed to be towed by electric bike or even a pedal-powered one, if your legs were strong enough and up to the task. When not used for camping, it could be used as a plain bike cargo trailer, doubling up the functionality you got for the money.
The B Turtle, which you might also find spelled as B-Turtle, was launched in 2018 by Austrian tent specialist GentleTent and, for a few years afterwards, enjoyed great success. This was no starry-eyed startup promising the world and then discovering that "wanting" and "doing" were two, very different things; this was a company that launched a product and took it internationally, both to sell and to rent.
At one point, the B Turtle was available in Germany, its native Austria (of course), Sweden, the Netherlands, and even Ireland. You could either buy a unit or, if you were strapped for cash or still undecided, you could rent one to try out and see how it fared.
Photo: YouTube/Atik Family The first signs of trouble appeared when the e-bike bubble began losing air. By May 2024, GentleTent had gone through one bankruptcy filing and one restructuring, but not even that was enough to help it through the hard times. One year later, in May 2025, the company filed for bankruptcy for one last time and went into liquidation.
That means that the B Turtle, perhaps the neatest bike caravan ever created, slipped off the map. Production (obviously) shut down and all stock vanished, though you can probably still find a unit in good condition on the second market.
And that brings us to the video below: a rare, recent, real-life camping experience with the B Turtle, courtesy of content creators Atik Family. The Atik couple often try out the newest motorhomes and camping solutions, in partnership with select manufacturers and distributors, but this one is a true surprise.
Photo: GentleTent Somehow, they found a B Turtle and took it out on a windy overnight outing, getting to see for themselves what exactly made this product better than any other bikepacking product on the market.
For us, it's a great occasion to remember a bike microcaravan that had all the right ingredients, but one – affordability –, while we take a trip down memory lane.
The B Turtle was a heavy-duty bike cargo trailer with 12-inch wheels, a slide-out storage box and the tent structure on top, folded down and packed neatly in a weatherproof zipped back. In road mode, it looked just like a bike cargo trailer would: compact and relatively lightweight , so it would not pose too much of an issue hauling around.
Photo: GentleTent Exact dimensions for the B Turtle in travel mode were 113 x 73.5 x 79 cm (44.5 x 29 x 31 inches), with an empty weight of 29-kg (64-pound).
GentleTent said that setup at camp was a matter of 15 minutes, which included inflating the tent superstructure and anchoring all the parts to the ground for safety. As you can see in the Atiks' video, that number is relative to the weather and the terrain you plan on setting up camp. Obviously, setting up a tent in windy weather is not going to be that easy.
The B Turtle came with adjustable support legs, but you still had to anchor it like a traditional tent . Once that part was out of the way, inflating the upper part and the mattress was done by a 12V pump – now that was the easy part!
Photo: GentleTent The elevated platform held a two-person bed and it came with three zippered windows. In front, an awning-style section with an integrated floor created a lobby where you had full standing height, and that, in Atiks' case, became the dining room. A zippered flap offered you quick access to the cargo box under the mattress.
The tent was made of high-quality Tencate fabric and came with a separate storm cover, so GentleTent advertised it as water-, storm-, and wind-proof. You can tell from the most recent experience that it is, indeed, wind- and water-proof. The manufacturer also promised it was UV-resistant.
The B Turtle was imagined as a solution for bikepackers and, best of all, an upgrade over anything they had been offered until then. It was a shelter off the ground, with a comfortable double bed inside and a space that would serve as dining space and changing room, also protected from the elements.
Photo: GentleTent It was, because of all these, a solution that would make bikepacking comfortable for longer stretches, without feeling like you've been to hell and back. The Atiks' outing shows that, indeed, it was quite a nice solution for longer stays in nature, in pairs, on e-bikes.
As already noted, what ended the B Turtle dream was high pricing. When we first checked it out in 2022, one unit was selling for €3,499 (approximately $3,900 at the current exchange rate), which, you will agree, is a whole lot of money for a tent with two bike wheels.

But that doesn’t mean they are not keeping the headlines. The rumor mill believes they might still surprise us before the end of the year with the latest Audi RS6 Avant and sedan executive high-performance models, or at least with the potential Audi RS Q5 SUV and Sportback siblings.
They are also making the first cars in the world that no longer need a smartphone to run Spotify, training humanoid robots to take over certain grueling factory operations, focusing on the Q9’s world’s first curved digital OLED panel that’s as thin as human hair, and also announced they will be spending no less than $4 billion on a new US factory in Georgia to produce the large SUVs and create 4,500 new jobs, with manufacturing starting in the early 2030s.
As such, it’s no wonder that everyone is keeping an eye on the developments from Ingolstadt, including the members of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI. For example, Uygar, a "professional daydreamer" based in Turkey and known as ' uygarspots ' on social media, has taken note of the all-new direction of Audi as drafted by Massimo Frascella, Audi AG’s design director, who loves “design, watches, travel, and food.”
There’s no mention of cars in there, but the Chief Creative Officer at Audi AG has a manifesto for automobiles: it’s called ‘The Radical Next,’ a unifying philosophy, and the prime example of it is the recent Audi Concept C that has so far impressed the world when it was translated into reduced series production with the Audi Nuvolari plug-in hybrid supercar limited series.
Now, the virtual artist has decided to use Audi’s ethos together with the radical spirit of the 2000 Audi Rosemeyer concept. His latest unofficial, hypothetical design project is dubbed Audi Concept S and brings the latter into the near 2030s with the same longtail allure and gilded design, but now applied to geometrically edgy shapes rather than slim and rounded elements.
The CGI wedge shape is well consecrated, and the Audi Concept S has a straight ‘face’ with a vertical-cut grille and tall side front intakes, while the cockpit is now of the ‘visor’ variety with wraparound glass elements that delete the front A-pillars for the sake of design. Around the back, the louvers hint at a mid-engine setup, and the humongous rear diffuser with dual tall exhaust outlets make it clear that it’s an ICE or hybrid powertrain. Barrier Blue Pontiac Bonneville Convertible Looks Better at 60 Than It Did Back in 1966
22 photos
Photo: Vanguard Motor Sales
This 1966 Pontiac Bonneville Convertible has recently walked out of the restoration shop, rocking head-turning blue paint over a blue interior and V8 firepower. Never a garage queen, the car has over 94,000 miles on the clock and is longing to be driven.
Finished in what Pontiac called Barrier Blue Metallic and sporting a white power-operated convertible top over a Morrokide interior, this 1966 Pontiac Bonneville probably looks better than it did the day it rolled off the production line of the Pontiac Assembly Plant in Michigan. In the meantime, many of its siblings rot in barns or junkyards, begging for restoration .
General Motors built 135,331 Bonnevilles in 1966, with the rarest body style (only 3,000 units built) being the four-door six-seat station wagon. Meanwhile, the two-door convertible, like this car right here, came second, with 16,229 examples, accounting for 12% of all Bonnevilles built that year.
The Pontiac Bonneville was built on General Motors' full-sized B-body platform and sat on a stretched, exclusive 124-inch (3,150-millimeter) wheelbase that was 3 inches (76.2 millimeters) longer than that of the entry-level Pontiac Catalina.
Photo: Vanguard Motor Sales The open-top variant came with the rakish fender lines, heavy ribbed lower-body chrome trim, and sleek rear fender skirts that elongated the vehicle visually. In the meantime, the cabin put on a premium show. A real wood-veneered instrument panel was integrated directly into the dashboard.
Pontiac also offered a tilt steering column, a remote mirror control, an automatic vacuum-operated trunk release, and the Wonder Touch power steering. To enhance the premium label, the power-operated convertible top featured a tempered glass rear window rather than the usual plastic.
The Bonneville convertible is set in motion by the 389 cubic-inch (6.4-liter) V8, with distinct factory ratings, depending on the transmission. This car comes with the Turbo Hydra-matic automatic transmission, which means the V8 pushes out 325 horsepower (330 metric horsepower) and 429 pound-feet (582 Newton meters) of torque.
This exact same engine, but with the factory Tri-Power option and dialed up to produce 360 horsepower (365 metric horsepower), was under the hood of the Pontiac GTO, the absolute pioneer of the American muscle car era, debuting on October 1, 1963.
Photo: Vanguard Motor Sales However, for the Bonneville, it was enough to make the convertible accelerate from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 8.4 seconds (the four-speed manual was over a second quicker) and max out at 119 mph (192 kph). Power brakes and power steering are also on the menu.
The Pontiac Bonneville, which has recently been through a frame-off restoration, is equipped with air conditioning. The ultra-thin, two-spoke steering wheel frames a speedometer scaled up to 120 mph (193 kph) and an odometer indicating 94,313 miles (151,782 kilometers). It may not sound like much of a globetrotter considering that the car saw the light of day 60 years ago. However, it shows that it is no garage queen.
Now, this no-garage-queen is in search of a new home and an owner who will drive it until its wheels fall off. Vanguard Motors listed it with a price of $119,900. That is far above the average. classic.com indicates that impeccably restored Bonnevilles reaching concours level can go well beyond the $60,000 on the collector car market. But this one right here sits well above the standard market average
Back in 1966, customers who wanted to go home with a Pontiac Bonneville Convertible had to pay a starting price of $3,586. Adjusted for inflation, that would be roughly $35,600. That is Toyota Camry Hybrid money.

Car Hunter Finds Rare 1989 Trans Am Pace Car, It's a Spectacular Time Capsule With a Carfax Secret
57 photos
Photo: YouTube/Dennis Collins
When Pontiac introduced the Firebird in 1967, the division sought an aggressive contender for the booming American pony car war – one that could fight the Mustang, the Camaro, and the Cougar in showrooms, and on the street. The Barracuda wasn’t much of a rival, much to the chagrin of Ma’ Mopar, but Pontiac wasn’t going for small fish.
Two years later, the Trans Am arrived. As with many other occurrences in life, one thing led to another, and twenty years later, the Firebird was pacing Indy 500. In pure stock form, no hidden catch, no nothing. And this survivor could tell a lot of stories, considering it’s one of the 1,555 examples built as a 20th Anniversary Limited Edition examples that replicated the final Pontiac pace car to run at Indianapolis.
Which brings us to the car showcased in Dennis Collins’ latest YouTube find. The Texan car hunter and his lead mechanic, Alex Bohling, travel near Quinlan, Texas, to inspect a 26,000-mile 1989 Turbo Trans Am owned by a longtime friend of Dennis. A diehard V8 enthusiast who once lost a street race to a Buick GNX, Thomas admitted he initially harbored a prejudice against six-cylinder engines until experiencing this Pontiac firsthand.
Thomas acquired the unrestored, garage-kept Texas survivor from a local owner who had mistakenly filled the tank with regular unleaded gasoline instead of the mandatory premium fuel. Sitting dirty in his shop, the coupe retained its original Production Automotive Services underhood stickers, the factory asbestos heat-shield bag wrapping the oversized coolant reservoir, and a functioning dashboard boost gauge alongside an aftermarket pillar pod.
Photo: YouTube/Dennis Collins Despite sporting hand-painted pinstripes and factory gold cross-lace wheels that a previous caretaker had spray-painted black to mimic a Buick GNX, the vehicle remained mechanically unmodified. Performing a cold start after the car sat for three days, the turbocharged powerplant fired up with zero warning lights, maintaining between 70 and 80 psi of oil pressure and running cool at all times.
I don’t mean that in the swagger-boasting sense of the expression, but in the most mechanically literal meaning: the engine’s coolant stayed at around 160 degrees Fahrenheit, which is about 71°C. Not bad at all for a car built nearly 40 years ago, and sparsely driven in good weather only. Which is still a lot better than other 1989 Trans Am pace cars, which are pampered garage-art exhibits with four-digit readings on the odometer. If this car was built for anything, it was for going very fast.
Taking Alex Bohling for a test drive, Thomas demonstrated how the coupe effortlessly reached 90 mph under light throttle, spinning its rear tires while tracking straight and cornering sharply. Impressed by the fade-free 1LE brakes, supportive pneumatic lumbar leather seats, and fierce midrange pull, Bohling confirmed that the driving experience completely erased any perception of a sluggish six-cylinder engine.
Photo: YouTube/Dennis Collins Following the demonstration, Dennis Collins finalized his strong cash offer, with Thomas generously knocking 1,000 dollars off the agreed price out of friendship. Upon bringing the Pontiac back to their Wylie, Texas, facility and placing it on a lift, Collins and Bohling discovered immaculate, rust-free floorboards alongside a minor Carfax blemish involving a past front-right bumper tap that left all factory VIN-stamped body panels untouched.
To restore the exterior to showroom specification, the duo sourced a missing Indianapolis 500 windshield header decal and sent the 16-inch aluminum wheels to a shop in Dallas to have the black paint stripped and the original gold finish restored. While measuring the rims, stamped for Front-only and Rear-only placement, Bohling solved a lingering mystery about the car’s alleged different tire sizes for front and back.
As it turns out, the 1989 Trans Am uses identical 245/55 R15s on all four corners. However, there is a hidden catch: the same rubbers sit on zero-millimeter front offset rims versus a 16-millimeter rear offset, to clear the massive twin-piston Corvette front brake calipers. Speaking of which, the pace car edition had the quick-release pads fitted, in case the race demanded its presence on the track for longer periods, and the hard braking sessions would wear the brake pads too much.
Photo: YouTube/Dennis Collins Which wasn’t that hard of a job for a car built around the same turbo V6 that had made the 1987 Buick GNX a street legend. Except the Pontiac engineers actually made that 3.8-liter motor even more unhinged for the 1989 season. It was a fitting homage paid to the original Trans Am that had broken ground two decades earlier.
In 1969, engineers elevated the Firebird vision by launching the Trans Am performance and appearance package, named directly after the Sports Car Club of America racing series. Despite paying a five-dollar royalty to the sanctioning body for every vehicle sold, Pontiac never actually campaigned the original model in the championship because its engine exceeded the strict 5.0-liter displacement limit.
Across its first two generations, the Trans Am evolved from a raw muscle machine into an undisputed pop-culture icon. While rival manufacturers abandoned performance during the restrictive emissions era of the 1970s, Pontiac doubled down with massive 7.5-liter (455 Super Duty, anyone?) engines and flamboyant Screaming Chicken hood decals.
Photo: YouTube/Dennis Collins By 1982, the third-generation F-body platform arrived, shifting the engineering focus from brute cubic inches toward wind-tunnel aerodynamics, fuel injection, forced induction, and nimble chassis dynamics to meet modern automotive demands.
That technological evolution reached an extraordinary peak in 1989 when Pontiac celebrated the twentieth birthday of its legendary performance moniker. Often hailed by enthusiasts as the ultimate sleeper of the late 1980s, this white coupe bridged the gap between vintage Detroit muscle and contemporary forced-induction engineering.
For the 1989 model year, Pontiac manufactured a total of 64,409 Firebirds across all trim levels. That figure included 31,876 base Firebirds, 16,670 Formula models, and 396 convertibles distributed across the lineup. Within the high-performance tier, the division assembled 5,701 standard Trans Am coupes alongside 8,081 luxurious Trans Am GTA models.
Photo: YouTube/Dennis Collins Standing at the absolute pinnacle of this production run was the limited-edition 20th Anniversary Turbo Trans Am: 1,555 units in total. Of those, five were early pre-production pilot cars pulled randomly from the Van Nuys assembly line, leaving 1,550 regular production examples for the public. Every showroom model wore Cameo White paint over a Saddle tan interior, leaving buyers with only two factory options.
As showcased by Dennis Collins, the vast majority of customers selected the fully loaded configuration pairing removable Lexan T-tops with leather seating, accounting for 1,324 identical cars built. The remaining production breakdown underscores the extreme rarity of alternative cabin and roof combinations within the anniversary series. 187 examples left the factory equipped with T-tops and cloth upholstery, a specification utilized for the official track festival fleet.
For purists seeking maximum structural rigidity without removable roof panels, Pontiac constructed 24 hardtop coupes with leather interiors and a mere 15 base hardtop models featuring cloth seats, while three cars were later converted into convertibles.
Photo: YouTube/Dennis Collins This special edition was engineered specifically to pace the 73rd running of the Indianapolis 500 in May 1989. Remarkably, it became the first vehicle in the history of the Brickyard capable of pacing the field straight off the showroom floor without any mechanical or performance modifications.
Officials merely installed strobe lights and safety harnesses before sending the coupe onto the oval, where Brazilian driver Emerson Fittipaldi ultimately captured the checkered flag under caution.
Production Automotive Services modified the 3.8-liter powerplant with higher-flowing cylinder heads derived from a transverse front-wheel-drive architecture to clear the tight F-body shock towers. Those upgrades were paired with a custom cross-drilled crankshaft, dished pistons yielding an 8.0:1 compression ratio, and stainless-steel exhaust headers.
Photo: YouTube/Dennis Collins Forced induction came courtesy of a Garrett T3 turbocharger working alongside a heavy-duty air-to-air intercooler featuring 12 fins per inch, matching the specification of the legendary Buick GNX. Pushing a maximum boost pressure of 16.5 psi through sequential multi-port fuel injection, the engine carried an official factory rating of 250 hp at 4,400 rpm and 340 lb-ft of torque at 2,800 rpm.
General Motors purposefully underrated that output to protect the internal hierarchy of the 245 hp Chevrolet Corvette. Independent dynamometer testing quickly revealed the truth behind Pontiac's conservative marketing claims. In reality, the modified six-cylinder engine generated over 300 hp at the flywheel, channeling all of its fury through a specially calibrated, hand-tagged Turbo Hydramatic 200-4R 4-speed automatic transmission equipped with a lockup torque converter.
Power reached the pavement via an Australian-built Borg-Warner 9-bolt limited-slip rear axle featuring a 3.27:1 final drive gear ratio, while heavy-duty 1LE dual-piston aluminum front calipers handled braking duties.
Photo: YouTube/Dennis Collins Those mechanical ingredients translated into blistering real-world performance that humbled exotic European sports cars costing three times its 31,000-dollar sticker price. Weighing 3,346 pounds, the 1989 Turbo Trans Am rocketed from 0 to 60 mph in just 4.6 seconds during contemporary magazine evaluations.
It demolished the standing quarter-mile in 13.4 seconds at 101 mph and pressed onward to an aerodynamics-aided top speed of 162 mph, cementing its legacy as the fastest American production car of 1989. The first one to walk onto the Brickyard in a white jacket and immediately pull the rein on all the open-wheel missiles with nothing more than a borrowed set of lights.

6-Star Roulette Ticket Is Up for Grabs This Week in Gran Turismo 7
24 photos
Photo: autoevolution
I just got a message from a fellow Greek RX-7 owner today. I’ve never spoken to him before, but I had definitely seen his Initial D-themed FC. It seems like we have common friends, which isn’t unusual given how few of us live in this part of the world. And he’s planning to visit me for a drive up the Transalpina touge.
Now, I’m more than happy to host and show him around, but he’s coming in November. By that time, the mountain will be covered in snow, and I don’t have winter tires for my Mazda RX-8.
I’ve been debating whether I should buy a set for it or not, knowing full well what taking it out in the snow will lead to.
Anyway, I’ll let you know how it goes in a few days. Until then, more virtual practice for me as I’m still stuck in bed with a sore back.
The new Weekly Challenges are available, and the grand prize is a 6-star roulette ticket. I didn’t stop there, as I also wanted to perform a turbo test with my McLaren F1 race car at Le Mans.
Sunday Cup Photo: autoevolution We’ve got two Japanese venues on the list for this week, but only one of them is a replica of a real-world racetrack.
Autopolis International Racing Course has two layouts, and we’ll be racing on the Shortcut Course which is only 1.87 miles/3,022 meters long.
I haven’t driven my Lamborghini Diablo GT in quite some time, and it already had the right livery for the location. With 834 bhp on tap, I went in too hot and found myself in the gravel twice on the first lap.
It’s definitely too much for the 380 PP Sunday Cup event, but it’s the best way to get it over with in less than 150 seconds. Expect to score 25,000 credits if you win!
European FR Challenge Photo: autoevolution I thought about the same approach for the European FR Challenge at the Nurburgring GP track. I noticed most of the cars on the grid were
BMWs, and I felt the sudden urge to “teach” them a lesson in a lightly-tuned Mercedes-Benz 190 E 2.5-16 Evolution II '91. I found out there was another one involved in the race, trying to be gentle with my throttle inputs on SS tires in the rain.
Once I was in the lead I felt no more pressure from my opponents, and I started thinking about the BMWs we still don’t have in the game after all these years.
The M5 E60 is on its way with part two of Spec IV, but there are plenty of other unexplored options out there: the E31 8 Series, the old Z3 M Coupe, and the X5 Le Mans. If you have any other suggestions I’d be happy to hear them.
Time Trial Photo: autoevolution This week’s Special Race is a short Time Trial at the High Speed Ring in Japan. Polyphony is sending us in with a 2011 Lamborghini Aventador LP 700-4 which means there’s plenty of power available.
It’s a fairly big car though, and you should be careful in choosing your braking points. Yes, you will have to use the brakes on this reverse layout.
Remember, any contact with the wall will immediately invalidate your attempt and have you start from scratch. It came as no surprise that user holl01 was the world leader when I signed in, with a 43.688 fast lap.
That’s almost three seconds than the target for Gold, while the Bronze Reward needs you to cross the finish line in under 50.7 seconds. I crashed the first two times, and my third attempt was the lucky one.
American Clubman Cup 700 Photo: autoevolution We have two 700 PP races on the “menu” this week, and you won’t have to worry about the tire wear and fuel consumption for the American Clubman Cup event. It makes perfect sense to have it at Michelin Raceway Road Atlanta, and seven laps will take a little over 10 minutes.
I could choose one of 13 vehicles in my garage, and the early 2000s Ford GT was the most enticing option. I could even push it close to 700 hp without using a supercharger and without going over the PP limit.
With 99 pages of custom liveries available for it, the Falken look was the first one that caught my attention. This car is a complete sledgehammer, and that’s not always a good thing. Anyway, it’s always fun and annoying to see that RCR Civic in the lead.
I understand a US tuner created this car, but that doesn’t mean it’s an American machine. I scored 90,000 credits for the win, and spent it right away on buying a new car for the next event.
World Touring Car 700 Photo: autoevolution I just didn’t want to use another one of my Group 4 machines for this 10-lap battle at Brands Hatch. I remember the Nissan Silvia spec-R Aero (S15) Touring Car is also a good match for this class and didn’t mind spending 350,000 credits for it again.
I must have finished this race at least a dozen times before, which reminds me of how badly we need Polyphony to act on the topic. The C-West livery is one of the best options for the S15 if you ask me, and I didn’t even bother with a turbo upgrade.
I needed four and a half laps to get into P1, and then pitted just moments later as I was all out of gas. Can we take pit stop photos already? I see no reason why it can’t be done. My best lap was my last one, and after 16 minutes and 39 seconds I walked away with an extra 110K in my virtual bank account.
To top it off, the 6-Star Roulette Ticket added one million more credits to it, which is why I finally bought that Xiaomi VGT car. I don’t plan on driving it, but it’s also in the way of me collecting all the vehicles in the game.
McLaren F1 @ Le Mans Photo: autoevolution I still 11 of them to get there, which means I’ll have to spent about 200 more million credits. That’s quite painful to think of, considering I’ve raised 516 million in four years. I knew I could get a turbo upgrade for the McLaren F1 Race Car, and I thought it could come in handy down the main straight.
I had high hopes of hitting 248 mph/400 kph, which is why I opted for the No Chicane layout and also used a gearbox with adjustable settings. That’s because on my first stint, it topped out at 190 mph/306 kph. The gear adjustment wasn’t that effective, as I found out the new limit was 195 mph/315 kph.
I assumed it might have had something to do with the aero settings, but didn’t do anything about them to find out. I needed three minutes and 35 seconds for the complete lap, just before upgrading to 789 bhp thanks to the top-level turbo.
Sixth gear proved useless again, as fifth provided the means to push the car to 212 mph/341 kph. The result? I improved by eight seconds per lap, and I’ll have to take it back to the Nurburgring for another test there as well.

Once again, it is time for HPC Career Notes, our monthly feature that’s designed to keep you up-to-date on the latest career developments for individuals in the HPC community, including promotion, new company hires, and accolade. Check in each month for an updated list and you may even come across someone you know, or better yet, yourself!
Michael Garland and Nathan Bell
Nathan Bell (l) and Michael Garland
Nvidia’s Michael Garland and Google’s Nathan Bell were awarded the SC26 Test of Time Award for their SC09 presentation on sparse computing, which was based on their paper titled “Implementing Sparse Matrix-Vector Multiplication on Throughput-Oriented Processors.”
Sparse matrix-vector multiplication is an important operation in computational science, as it appears repeatedly in methods for solving large-scale linear systems and eigenvalue problems across scientific and engineering applications. However, sparse matrices remain a challenge for parallel hardware, such as GPUs.
Rather than treating all sparse matrices in the same way, Garland and Bell considered different sparsity patterns and the data formats best suited to them, which can reduce the execution and memory divergence caused by irregular matrix structures. Their results demonstrated that sparse computation can be mapped successfully onto GPU architectures. In their study, Garland and Bell showed that sparse matrices could be run with high levels of memory bandwidth utilization on the Nvidia GeForce GTX 285.
Garland, who is currently is a senior director of programming research at Nvidia, will look back on the paper and the ensuing work in his SC26 presentation titled “Twenty Years of Sparsity on GPUs.”
Caira Anderson
Caira Anderson, a doctoral student in the Center for Applied Mathematics at Cornell University, has completed a three-month graduate fellowship practicum at the Mathematics and Computer Science (MCS) division of Argonne National Laboratory studying computational methods and software for large-scale scientific simulation.
Caria Anderson
Anderson, who is a recipient of a DOE Computational Science Graduate Fellowship (CSGF), chose Argonne for her practicum because of its strength in applied mathematics, scientific computing, and HPC software
“MCS is a natural fit for my interests in numerical methods and scientific software,” Anderson said. ​“I was excited by the chance to learn how solver methods are developed, tested, and used in large-scale scientific computing applications.”
Anderson’s thesis work focuses on numerical methods for the linear ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) eigenvalue problem, which is used to study the stability of plasma equilibria in application areas such as fusion energy, per Gail Piper’s writeup on the Argonne site . During her practicum, Anderson studied the performance of a fully implicit Runge–Kutta (IRK) time-stepping method implemented in PETSc, Argonne’s suite of software for scientific computing.
While she focused on numerical methods and scientific computing, Anderson also has been exploring AI tools, such as Claude. “For this kind of work, AI can be useful as a coding and reasoning aid, but I feel it is still important to understand the mathematical formulation, verify the implementation and test the results carefully,” she said. ​“In my experience, AI tools are most useful when they support that process rather than replace it.”
Wei Jia Ong
Wei Jia Ong
Wei Jia Ong, a staff scientist at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL), was named a 2026 recipient of the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Science Early Career Research Program award.
With support from the award, Ong will pursue an integrated approach to understanding the origins of p-nuclei, a type of stable nuclei with an excess of protons. “P-nuclei are extremely interesting because they cannot be made by neutron-capture reactions, which is how more than 99% of stable nuclei are made in stars,” she said, according to a story by LLNL’s Ashley Piccone on the LLNL website.
While scientists approximately understand the mechanisms behind neutron capture and the formation of neutron-rich isotopes, how and where p-nuclei are made is still a topic of contention.
The Early Career Research Program provides five-year awards to exceptional early-career researchers at U.S. academic institutions, National Laboratories, and Office of Science User Facilities to stimulate new research directions in mission critical areas supported by DOE’s Office of Science.
“Winning this award is an incredible honor, and I have to thank the vast number of colleagues who helped me develop the ideas and improve the proposal,” said Ong. “I can’t wait to see what we find!”
Michael McQuade, Matt Long, and Quan Nguyen
(l to r) Michael McQuade, Matt Long, and Quan Nguyen
HPC software developer Parallel Works made several personnel moves in the past month, including the promotions of Michael McQuade to VP of engineering, Matt Long to lead mission engineering, and Quan Nguyen to director of engineering.
As VP of engineering, McQuade will lead the continued development and advancement of Parallel Works Activate platform. McQuade has helped develop that product as director of engineering.
As director of mission engineering, Long will oversee the teams that deploy, operate, and support customer HPC and AI environments. He will focus on strengthening customer engagement, optimizing infrastructure performance and ensuring organizations can reliably execute demanding computational workloads.
Nguyen, meanwhile, will help to lead development of the Activate platform as the eirector of engineering. Previously, he served as engineering team lead.
“Most HPC and AI projects don’t stall because the hardware isn’t there,” said Matthew Shaxted, CEO of Parallel Works. “They stall because no one owns the integration, the tuning and unexpected failures. That’s what mission engineering is for, and it’s why we’re putting experienced leaders in charge of it.
“Michael, Matt and Quan have dedicated years to helping researchers and engineers overcome complex HPC and AI challenges with world-class solutions,” Shaxted continued. “These promotions position them to expand that impact, bringing their expertise and innovative approaches to an even broader range of customers.”
John McKillop
John McKillop
Storage software provider Hammerspace has appointed John McKillop, a sales executive with a quarter of a century experience in tech sales, to the position of vice president of Americas sales.
McKillop previously was the senior vice president of global sales and senior vice president of Americas sales at storage vendor Quantum. Prior to that, he was chief revenue officer at Openprise, where he helped helping enterprises optimize go-to-market operations through data orchestration, automation and AI.
“What attracted me to Hammerspace is the combination of differentiated technology, an exceptional team and the momentum already underway,” McKillop said. “The market opportunity is enormous, and Hammerspace is uniquely positioned to capture it. My focus is on accelerating that growth by scaling our sales organization, expanding our strategic partnerships and helping more customers realize the value of AI anywhere.”
“We’ve experienced phenomenal growth this year,” said Hammerspace is excited to bring McKillop on board, said Hammerspace’s Chief Business Officer Tony Asaro. “He has a great track record of success, scaling sales organizations and building the partnerships needed to turn market leadership into sustained revenue growth,” he said.
Wahid Bhimji and Shashank Subramanian
Shashank Subramanian (l) and Wahid Bhimji
Wahid Bhimji and Shashank Subramanian, two members of the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC)’s Real-Time Synchrotron Imaging Analysis Team, have received the at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory Director’s Awards for exceptional achievements in science.
Bhimji and Subramanian received the Director’s Award “for foundational work building the Advanced Light Source (ALS) imaging superfacility, culminating in the delivery of real-time, AI-driven analysis of microtomography experiments leveraging DOE’s high-performance networks and computing infrastructure,” LBNL said in a press release .
According to LBNL, the collaboration between ALS and NERSC has “dramatically accelerated” and improved the process where massive amounts of data captured at the ALS are analyzed at NERSC and returned to ALS researchers in near-real time. The lab says that its success could also pave the way for similar integration between experimental facilities and HPC resources underpinning the U.S. Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission project, particularly its American Science Cloud initiative.
“It’s a great honor to receive this award; it’s the culmination of the work of many people across NERSC and ALS, over many years, to enable real-time HPC workflows for science,” said Bhimji. “These approaches now form the foundation of efforts in the American Science Cloud and Genesis Mission which could further enable transformative science in the coming years.”
Rekha Rao
Rekha Rao (center) receiving her award in Munich in July 2026
Sandia National Laboratories recently announced that Rehka Rao is the first employee to receive dual fellowships, including for the Society of Rheology and the International Association for Computational Mechanics.
She is the first Sandia employee to ever be elected a fellow of the IACM. She also served as the first female president of the U.S. Association for Computational Mechanics, Sandia tells us in a press release .
Rao accepted her IACM fellowship at the World Congress on Computational Mechanics in Munich, Germany, which brought 5,000 researchers together from around the world in July. “Being the first Sandia fellow at IACM and getting international recognition was just really amazing,” Rao said. “Especially because this is not only for my service but also for my technical achievements.”
Rao will receive her fellowship recognition from the Society of Rheology in late October.
Rao discovered her passion for research and problem-solving during her undergraduate studies at the University of California, Berkeley. She has spent her entire career at Sandia, having joined in 1990 with a doctorate in chemical engineering, specializing in computational fluid dynamics.
After starting out in nuclear waste disposal, she moved to engineering sciences. Much of her career has focused on deterrence work, including the B-61 nuclear bomb.
“Every time they build a new encapsulated part, they will run the models to make sure the molds fill well with minimal defects,” Rao said. “You have specific foam parts that need to be high-quality structural supports. We have developed multiphysics models to understand the fluid flow, solidification, and aging. Electronic components are encapsulated, so the foam must survive drop or bumps. These models help do that.”
Peter Shor
Peter Shor
Zapata Quantum has appointed Peter Shor and other notable scientists to its Scientific Advisory Board (SAB). Shor is the MIT mathematician whose landmark 1994 algorithm, now known as Shor’s algorithm, showed how quantum computers could solve a major computational problem far faster than the best-known classical methods, helping launch the modern field of quantum computing.
“Quantum computers will only be as useful as the applications we run on them. As hardware matures toward fault tolerance, it’s critical that we discover and develop new algorithms to truly unlock the power of this new technology,” said Dr. Shor. “I’m excited about the work Zapata is doing in this area and look forward to helping guide those efforts.”
In addition to Dr. Shor, other distinguished scientists joining the SAB include Alexandru Paler, Associate Professor of Computer Science at Aalto University in Finland; Simon Devitt, Professor and Director of the Centre for Quantum Software and Information (QSI) at the University of Technology, Sydney; and Artur Izmaylov, Professor of Theoretical and Computational Chemistry at the University of Toronto.
“Dr. Shor’s work is the reason this entire field exists,” said Sumit Kapur, CEO of Zapata Quantum. “His discovery of quantum algorithmic advantage is the foundational proof point the industry has been built upon, and having his guidance regarding our scientific direction is strong validation of our approach.”
Mark Long
Mark Long
Supermicro appointed seasoned finance executive Mark Long as senior vice president and chief financial officer. Long will report directly to the computer maker’s CEO, Charles Liang.
Long has more than three decades of experience across the technology sector, including a stint at Western Digital, where he led financial management, investor relations and corporate strategy as CFO and chief strategy officer. He also served as co-founder and partner of Prime Impact Capital, a technology-focused investment firm. Long also was a senior vice president of strategy and corporate development at Hitachi Global Storage Technologies.
“I am honored to join Supermicro as it continues to build on its leadership in AI and high-performance infrastructure,” Long said. “Charles has built a remarkable company, and I look forward to partnering closely with him and the executive team to scale the business effectively and efficiently – strengthening our financial foundation while supporting continued innovation, growth, and long-term value creation for shareholders.”
Weikuan Yu
Weikuan Yu
Florida State University Professor of Computer Science Weikuan Yu will serve as a director within the Office of Advanced Cyberinfrastructure at the National Science Foundation (NSF). NSF program director for at least one year starting in Fall 2026.
In the role, Yu collaborate with researchers and other program directors to help manage NSF programs and oversee federal research investments related to his expertise in AI, powerful computing systems, large-scale data management and computing infrastructure.
Yu joined FSU’s Department of Computer Science in 2015 and has served as associate chair for research and held the Mainline Information Systems Endowed Professorship. He also led the Department of Computer Science as chair for three years.
“It’s a great honor to represent FSU at the national level and contribute to federal investments in advanced cyberinfrastructure and national AI research resources,” Yu said. “This opportunity comes at an especially exciting time, as AI is rapidly reshaping science, technology and society. The role gives me an opportunity to step back and look more broadly at where our research community is heading, particularly how national computing, AI and data infrastructure can enable scientific discovery and serve the larger research community.”
Terry Benzel
Terry Benzel
Terry Benzel was voted as IEEE Computer Society’s 2028 president, the group announced recently. Benzel is the managing director of the Information Sciences Institute (ISI) at the University of Southern California and an IEEE Fellow recognized for leadership in cybersecurity experimentation.
A long-time IEEE CS volunteer, Benzel has contributed through conferences, publications, technical communities, governance, and strategic initiatives, the group says. In addition to being the society’s current vice president, she represents the society on the multi-society CLEAR (Community-Led Ethics for Accountability in Research) Task Force and leads the society’s Ethics and Integrity initiative. An IEEE Fellow, Benzel has received numerous IEEE CS honors, including the Golden Core Recognition, Outstanding Service Award, Outstanding Community Service Award, and Continuing Service Award.
Benzel garnered 2,539 votes, compared with 1,305 votes cast for Saurabh Bagchi, a professor at Purdue University, and chair of its computer engineering division whose research contributions lie in reliable and secure computing and co-founder of startup KeyByte LLC.
Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award Winners
Ernest Orlando Lawrence
The Department of Energy announced nine recipients of the prestigious Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award for their exceptional contributions to research and development supporting the department’s missions in science, energy, and national security. Ernest Orlando Lawrence was a Berkeley Lab scientist who won the 1939 Nobel Prize in Physics for his invention of the cyclotron.
“From achieving fusion ignition to advancing critical materials and high-performance computing, these scientists and engineers are tackling some of our nation’s most complex challenges and translating groundbreaking research into real-world capabilities,” said Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “Their work strengthens our nation’s energy security, drives American innovation, and ensures the United States remains at the forefront of scientific discovery.”
The winners include:
Eric J. Schelter, University of Pennsylvania, in Atomic, Molecular, and Chemical Sciences. Schelter was honored for “fundamental chemical studies of energy-critical metals leading to new methods for their selective and sustainable separations.”
Patrick Chain, Los Alamos National Laboratory and New Mexico Consortium, in Biological and Environmental Sciences. Chain was honored for his “pioneering work in genomics and microbiome science, including discoveries of new bacterial-fungal interactions and revolutionizing the field by democratizing access to advanced bioinformatics tools.”
Samuel W. Williams, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, in Computer, Information, and Knowledge Sciences. Williams was honored for his “pioneering contributions in performance modeling, hardware/software design optimization, and novel computer architecture for high-performance computing, enabling modeling of complex computational solutions, and increasing analysis speed, simulation accuracy, and computational efficiency.”
Thomas Epps, III, University of Delaware, in Condensed Matter and Materials Sciences. Epps was honored for his “fundamental contributions to chemistry and materials science with applications in the chemical upcycling of polymeric waste, generation of high-performance materials from biomass feedstocks, and development of membranes for lithium-ion battery technologies.”
Gregg Beckham, National Laboratory of the Rockies and University of Colorado Boulder, in Energy Science and Innovation. Beckham was honored for his “transformative research in the conversion of lignocellulosic biomass and waste plastics via biology, chemistry, and engineering, yielding building blocks for sustainable fuels, chemicals, and materials.”
Andrea L. Kritcher, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, in Fusion and Plasma Sciences. Kritcher was honored for her “exceptional design efforts leading to the first-ever achievement of fusion ignition in the Laboratory, which is of major scientific impact to institutional and national missions, the private sector, and fusion interests within academia.”
Charles C. Polly, Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, High Energy Physics – Polly was honored for his “exceptional scientific and technical contributions to low-energy precision measurements in particle physics, most notably leadership of the experimental measurement of the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon with the Muon g-2 experiment.”
Michael Reed, Nevada National Security Site, in National Security and Nonproliferation. Reed was honored for his “vital contributions to national and international nuclear emergency response through the Advanced Visualization & Integration of Data (AVID) software, which broke existing paradigms by simultaneously fusing all radiological data into a single interface connected seamlessly to world-wide expertise.”
Lijuan Ruan, Brookhaven National Laboratory, in Nuclear Physics. Ruan was honored for her “outstanding leadership and ingenuity in the design, construction, and operation of novel detector systems in the STAR experiment, transforming dilepton final states into precision probes of heavy ion collisions.”
DOE will honor the recipients at a hybrid award ceremony in Washington, D.C., on November 13, 2026. The ceremony will be broadcast live online.
